summary: A BBN memo about problems with Telnet, the remote terminal protocol, starting from the question of who should echo typed characters. The authors work down to underlying principles and propose an alternative scheme for echoing. It is a design discussion that fed into later Telnet meetings, not a final specification.

eli5.summary: When you type on a faraway computer, who shows your letters back to you, you or the far computer? These people argued over a better way to decide.

questions: what is no echo in telnet
subtitle: Two BBN engineers propose letting either end of a Telnet connection suggest who echoes typed characters, and sketch bigger ideas on top.

tldr.problem: Telnet conventions barred the server from changing the echo mode, so servers and users were stuck in the wrong mode and had to remember each server's setup.
tldr.mechanism: Either side may request ECHO or NO ECHO, the other side confirms or refuses, and a connection starts in NO ECHO, so at most three commands are ever exchanged.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion memo, not a final specification. It argues for default implementation, negotiated options and symmetry, and volunteers to write a full Telnet specification on those lines.

today: RFC 435 is a discussion memo with no recorded status, and it updates RFC 318. It proposes ideas and does not itself define a standard.

sections.title: The Echoing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 435, from B. Cosell and D. Walden of BBN, collects Telnet issues that bothered the authors. It assumes Telnet is defined as suggested in RFC 318. The central issue is echoing: who displays the characters a user types, the user's own terminal (or local Host) or the remote server.

The authors observe that servers are tuned to handle terminals that either echo for themselves or do not, but not both. The existing conventions forbid the server from starting a change of echo mode. The authors understand that this rule was meant to prevent loops from races when both sides try to set an echo mode at once. They argue it burdens servers and makes users remember the right mode for each server.

They also recommend a separate STOP HIDING YOUR INPUT command, so hiding input is no longer multiplexed onto NO ECHO.
sections.eli5: Right now only the user may say who shows the typed letters, which is awkward. The authors want both sides to be able to ask.

sections.title: The Proposed Echo Scheme
sections.content:
The scheme rests on three assumptions: the server as well as the user can suggest the echo mode; every terminal can provide its own echoes, internally or through the local Host; and every server can run in a mode that assumes the terminal echoes for itself.

The commands ECHO and NO ECHO are reused. Sent by the server, ECHO means 'I'll echo to you'. Sent by the user, it means 'You echo to me'. NO ECHO means 'I'll not echo to you' or 'Don't you echo to me'.

  • Both sides assume a connection starts in NO ECHO mode.
  • Neither party can refuse a request to change into NO ECHO mode.
  • An unsolicited command may only request a change of mode.
  • A party changes mode only on an admissible request.
  • On receiving a command, a party replies with its echo mode, unless it did not have to change mode.

A refusal is the inverse command, which must be NO ECHO. The authors note that the procedure cannot loop, because at most three commands pass between the parties. A faulty implementation could still repeat a refused command, which they treat as an implementation fault.
sections.eli5: Either of you may say 'could you show the letters?'. The other says yes by doing it, or no by saying so. Because the answers are fixed, you cannot go back and forth forever.

sections.title: Principles and Further Ideas
sections.content:
The authors name three principles: default implementation (every option has a required default), negotiated options (both parties must agree), and symmetry (neither party should need to know whether it is the server or the user).

Applying them, the note floats further options as ideas without immediate urgency: line-at-a-time versus character-at-a-time mode, the end-of-line convention, hiding input, John Davidson's echoing scheme from RFC 357, and even the character set, with 7-bit USASCII as the default. A QUOTE character could let binary data share the connection, which might let higher-level protocols such as file transfer and graphics be built on Telnet.

For symmetry the TENEX group suggested four commands, I'LL ECHO TO YOU, YOU ECHO TO ME, DON'T ECHO TO ME and I'LL NOT ECHO TO YOU. The note then compacts these into four prefixes (WILL, WON'T, DO, DON'T) placed before one code per option. A site would handle the default 'NVT' mode and answer no to any option it does not understand, which makes options truly optional. The authors volunteer to specify such a Telnet at whatever level of complexity the community wants.
sections.eli5: Once you can ask politely, you can ask about other things too, like typing line by line. A computer can just say no to anything it does not know.

sections.title: A Sample TIP Implementation
sections.content:
An appendix shows how simply the basic scheme could be built into the TIP, a terminal-handling node. For each terminal the TIP keeps three state bits: P(hysical), whether the terminal echoes for itself; D(esired), the user's preferred mode; and A(ctual), the mode the connection is in.

On dial-up, P is set to match the terminal, D is set equal to it, and A is set to NO ECHO. When a connection opens, the TIP sends ECHO if the minimum of P and D differs from A, where NO ECHO is less than ECHO. Incoming requests set A to the minimum of the request, P and D, and the TIP acknowledges or refuses accordingly. Bigger Hosts might send these commands often, for example switching modes between a JOSS subsystem and DDT.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows a small computer that just remembers three yes-or-no notes and compares them to decide what to do.
